Running evals by hand occasionally instead of on every change.
Stopping at offline metrics without checking whether users are better off.

questions.question: How do you build an eval set?
questions.answer: Start from real or realistic inputs, cover common cases, edge cases and known failures, write expected outputs or grading criteria for each, and keep it versioned. Start with 50 to 200 examples and grow it from production failures. Keep a held-out portion that is never used for prompt tuning.

questions.question: How do you make LLM-as-judge reliable?
questions.answer: Give the judge a precise rubric and, where possible, a reference answer; ask for a short justification before the score; use pairwise comparison for subjective quality; swap answer order to control position bias; watch for length and self-preference bias; and calibrate against human labels, reporting agreement. Re-check calibration when the judge model changes.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you treat an LLM judge as a measurement instrument that needs calibration, and know its common biases and how to control them.
framework: Write a specific rubric with one criterion per score and concrete examples of each score.
Prefer pairwise or binary judgments over vague 1-10 scales.
Control known biases: position (swap the order and average), length and self-preference.
Ask for a short justification before the score, and use a low temperature.
Calibrate against human labels on a sample, report agreement, and re-check when the judge model or prompt changes.

follow_ups.q: What agreement level is good enough?
follow_ups.a: Close to the agreement between two human raters on the same task; if humans disagree a lot, the rubric needs work first.

common_mistakes: Using a vague overall quality score.
Not swapping positions in pairwise comparisons.
Trusting the judge without measuring agreement with humans.
Changing the judge model mid-experiment.

questions.question: Offline vs online evaluation: what is the difference?
questions.answer: Offline: run a fixed eval set before release to catch regressions. Online: measure live behavior through A/B tests, user feedback, task completion, escalation rates and sampled reviews. Both are needed: offline gates releases, online tells you whether users are actually better off.

questions.question: How do you A/B test an AI feature?
questions.answer: Randomize users (not requests) to variants, define a primary metric tied to user value (task success, retention, resolution rate) plus guardrail metrics (latency, cost, complaints), size the test for the effect you care about, and watch for novelty effects. Keep model, prompt and retrieval changes separable so you know what caused the result.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you can connect offline evaluation with online experiments and choose metrics that reflect user value rather than model scores.
framework: Gate with offline evals first so only candidates that pass reach users.
Pick one primary metric tied to user value, such as task success or resolution without escalation.
Add guardrail metrics: latency, cost per request, complaints, safety flags.
Randomize by user, size the test for the effect you care about, and fix the duration in advance.
Analyze honestly: avoid peeking, check segments, and read sampled conversations alongside the numbers.

follow_ups.q: Why randomize by user instead of by request?
follow_ups.a: Per-request switching gives users an inconsistent experience and contaminates behavioral metrics such as retention.

common_mistakes: Skipping offline evaluation and testing everything live.
Using model scores as the primary online metric.
Stopping the test as soon as it looks significant.
Ignoring cost and latency guardrails.

questions.question: What metrics do you track for a production LLM feature?
questions.answer: Quality (eval scores, user ratings, task success), safety (policy violations, refusals), latency (time to first token, total time at p50/p95/p99), cost (tokens and dollars per request), reliability (error, timeout and retry rates) and usage. Slice them by user segment and model version.

questions.question: What is benchmark contamination and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Test questions from a benchmark leaking into training data, which inflates scores without real capability. It is why public leaderboard results may not predict performance on your task. Use private, recently written eval sets and check for overlap when you fine-tune.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you read public benchmark scores critically and know how to protect your own evaluation from the same problem.
framework: Define it: benchmark questions or answers appear in a model's training data, so the score measures memory, not ability.
How it happens: benchmarks are published online and web-scale crawls pick them up, directly or through paraphrases.
Effect: inflated scores and misleading model comparisons.
Detection: n-gram overlap checks, testing on rephrased or newly written items, and comparing with performance on fresh data.
Protection: keep a private eval set built from your own tasks and refresh it over time.

follow_ups.q: Can your own eval set get contaminated?
follow_ups.a: Yes, if it leaks into fine-tuning data or you tune prompts against it repeatedly; keep a frozen hold-out portion.

common_mistakes: Choosing a model purely from leaderboard scores.
Publishing or sharing your private eval set.
Tuning prompts on the same set used for the final decision.
Assuming contamination only means exact copies; paraphrases count too.

questions.question: How do you evaluate hallucination or faithfulness?
questions.answer: Break the answer into individual claims and check each against the provided sources (with an NLI model or an LLM judge), then report the share of supported claims. Pair it with citation checks: does the cited passage actually contain the claim?

questions.question: What is regression testing for prompts and models?
questions.answer: Running the eval suite automatically in CI on every prompt, model or retrieval change and blocking the change if key metrics drop beyond a threshold. It turns prompt changes into reviewed code changes.

questions.question: How do you choose between two models for a feature?
questions.answer: Run both on your eval set and compare quality, then latency at your expected load, cost per successful task (not per token), context and tooling needs, data and compliance terms, and reliability of the provider. Often a cheaper model plus routing for hard cases wins.

questions.question: Design a customer-support assistant for a SaaS company.
questions.answer: Clarify scope (answer questions, take actions, or both), channels, volume and escalation rules. Components: RAG over help docs and past tickets with permission filters; account tools with read-only defaults and confirmation for changes; conversation memory; intent routing to a cheap model for simple questions; human handoff with full context; evals on resolution accuracy; monitoring of escalation and satisfaction. Discuss failure modes: stale docs, prompt injection through tickets, and wrong refunds.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you can structure an end-to-end LLM system: requirements, architecture, safe actions, escalation, evaluation and metrics, with sensible trade-offs.
framework: Clarify requirements: channels, languages, volume, which actions are allowed, latency target and when to hand off to humans.
Architecture: classify intent, retrieve from help docs and past resolved tickets, and call account tools with the user's permissions.
Generate grounded answers with citations; route low-confidence or sensitive cases to a human with a summary.
Guardrails: no unapproved refunds or account changes, PII handling, injection-resistant tool use.
Evaluate offline on real tickets, then track resolution rate, escalation quality, customer satisfaction, cost and latency.

follow_ups.q: How do you keep answers current when docs change?
follow_ups.a: Re-index on document updates, show source links, and flag answers whose sources were recently changed or removed.

common_mistakes: Jumping to the model choice before clarifying scope and allowed actions.
No escalation path or a hand-off that loses context.
Letting the model take account actions without permission checks.
Measuring only deflection instead of real resolution.

questions.question: Design an evaluation pipeline for an LLM product.
questions.answer: Versioned eval datasets, a runner that executes prompts/models in parallel with caching, graders (exact match, programmatic checks, calibrated LLM judges, human review queues), result storage per run, dashboards with diffs against the baseline, and CI gates. Feed production failures back into the dataset.

questions.question: Design a model-serving platform.
questions.answer: API gateway with auth, quotas and routing; model servers with continuous batching and paged KV cache (e.g. vLLM or TGI); autoscaling on queue depth and GPU utilization; streaming responses; per-tenant rate limits; health checks and fallbacks to another model or provider; and metrics for time to first token, tokens per second and cost.

questions.question: Design a document-processing (extraction) pipeline.
questions.answer: Ingest, then OCR or layout parsing, classify document type, extract fields with schema-constrained output, validate (types, cross-field rules, totals), score confidence, send low-confidence items to human review, and store with lineage back to the page. Measure field-level accuracy per document type.

questions.question: Design an LLM gateway for a company.
questions.answer: One internal endpoint in front of all providers: authentication, per-team keys and budgets, model routing and fallback, prompt and response logging with PII redaction, caching, rate limiting, usage and cost reporting, and policy enforcement. It gives central control and lets teams switch models without code changes.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you can design shared platform infrastructure for LLM use: reliability, cost control, security and observability across many teams.
framework: Unified API: one interface for many providers and self-hosted models, so teams do not integrate each one.
Access control: per-team keys, quotas, rate limits and budgets.
Routing: choose models by policy, with fallbacks on errors and timeouts, and retries with backoff.
Efficiency: response and prompt caching, and streaming passthrough.
Governance and observability: logging with PII redaction, cost attribution per team, data-residency rules and dashboards.

follow_ups.q: What is the biggest risk of a central gateway?
follow_ups.a: It becomes a single point of failure and a latency hop, so it needs redundancy, low overhead and a careful rollout.

common_mistakes: Forgetting per-team cost attribution and budgets.
Logging full prompts with personal data unredacted.
No fallback when a provider is down.
Adding heavy processing that increases latency on every request.

questions.question: Design a semantic search engine.
questions.answer: Ingestion and chunking, embeddings, an ANN index with metadata filters, hybrid lexical plus vector retrieval, re-ranking, snippets and highlighting, query understanding (spelling, synonyms), and click and relevance feedback for tuning. Evaluate with nDCG on labelled queries.

questions.question: Design a real-time content moderation system.
questions.answer: Layered: fast rules and hashes for known bad content, a small classifier for most traffic, and an LLM or human review for ambiguous cases; policy defined as labeled categories; latency budget per layer; appeals flow; and monitoring of precision and recall per category and language. Bias and over-blocking are as important as misses.

questions.question: How do you architect a multi-tenant AI platform?
questions.answer: Isolate tenant data at storage and retrieval (tenant ID filters enforced server-side, separate indexes for high-sensitivity tenants), per-tenant keys, quotas and cost tracking, per-tenant prompt or adapter configuration, noisy-neighbor protection, and audit logs. Never let one tenant's data enter another's prompt or cache.

questions.question: How do you design caching for LLM applications?
questions.answer: Exact-match response cache for repeated identical requests; provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes; semantic cache (embedding similarity above a strict threshold) for near-duplicate questions where answers do not depend on the user; embedding cache during ingestion. Include model and prompt versions in cache keys and set TTLs so answers do not go stale.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you know the different cache layers for LLM systems, their risks, and how to key and invalidate them safely.
framework: Exact-match response cache: key on a hash of model, version, full prompt and parameters.
Prompt (prefix) caching: keep the static part of prompts first so providers or the inference server can reuse computation.
Semantic cache: reuse answers for similar queries, with a high similarity threshold and only for safe, generic content.
Correctness: include permissions and tenant in keys, set expiry, and invalidate when source documents change.
Measure hit rate, savings, and the error rate of cached answers.

follow_ups.q: Why can a semantic cache be dangerous?
follow_ups.a: Similar-looking questions can need different answers, so it can serve a confidently wrong or another user's answer.

common_mistakes: Leaving the model version or parameters out of the cache key.
Sharing cached answers across users with different permissions.
Putting variable content at the start of the prompt, which defeats prefix caching.
Using a loose similarity threshold for semantic caching.

questions.question: How do you route queries across multiple models?
questions.answer: Classify each request by difficulty, task type or required capability (a rules layer or a small classifier), send easy requests to a cheap fast model and hard ones to a stronger model, and escalate when a verifier or confidence check fails. Measure quality and cost per route.

questions.question: How do you migrate a product from one model to another?
questions.answer: Run both on the eval set, adjust prompts for the new model, shadow-test on live traffic, compare quality, latency and cost, roll out gradually behind a flag with rollback, and keep monitoring. Re-embed if the embedding model changes.

questions.question: Design a code-assistant feature for an IDE.
questions.answer: Context gathering (current file, related files via retrieval over the repo, recent edits), a low-latency model for inline completion and a stronger one for chat or multi-file edits, streaming, a sandbox for running tests, and acceptance-rate and edit-survival metrics. Respect repository permissions and keep secrets out of prompts.

questions.question: How do you monitor an LLM system in production?
questions.answer: Log each request with prompt version, model, tokens, latency, cost and outcome; trace multi-step calls; dashboards and alerts on error rate, p95 latency, cost spikes and quality signals; sample conversations for review; and track user feedback. Redact PII in logs.

questions.question: How do you reduce LLM inference cost?
questions.answer: Route easy requests to smaller models, shorten prompts, use prompt caching for shared prefixes, cache responses, cap output length, batch offline work (batch APIs are usually discounted), and for self-hosting use quantization and continuous batching. Track cost per successful task.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you approach cost with measurement and a ranked list of levers, while protecting quality with evaluation.
framework: Measure: cost per request and per successful task, broken down by feature, model, input and output tokens.
Right-size models: route easy requests to smaller models and reserve large ones for hard cases.
Cut tokens: shorter prompts, fewer retrieved chunks, output length limits, and summarized history.
Reuse and batch: response and prefix caching, and batch APIs for offline jobs.
Self-hosted levers: quantization, continuous batching and high GPU utilization; re-run evals after every change.

follow_ups.q: Which lever do you try first?
follow_ups.a: Usually routing to smaller models and trimming tokens, since they need little infrastructure and often give the largest savings.

common_mistakes: Optimizing without a cost breakdown.
Measuring cost per call instead of per successful task.
Ignoring output tokens, which are often priced higher.
Cutting cost without re-running quality evals.

questions.question: How do you reduce latency?
questions.answer: Stream tokens, choose smaller or faster models for the first response, cut prompt length, parallelize retrieval and tool calls, cache, place servers near users, and use speculative decoding when self-hosting. Measure time to first token and total time separately.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you understand the parts of LLM latency and can pick fixes for each, including the user-perceived side.
framework: Measure the parts: time to first token (TTFT), tokens per second, and total time including retrieval and tools.
Stream output so users see progress immediately.
Shorten inputs (less prefill) and outputs (fewer decode steps); output length often dominates.
Use smaller or faster models for simple steps, and prefix caching for repeated prompt parts.
Remove serial steps: run retrieval and tool calls in parallel, and cut unnecessary chain steps.

follow_ups.q: Why does output length matter more than input length?
follow_ups.a: Prompt tokens are processed in parallel during prefill, while output tokens are generated one at a time.

common_mistakes: Optimizing without a latency breakdown.
Not streaming in user-facing flows.
Running independent calls sequentially.
Looking only at average latency instead of p95.

questions.question: How do you handle provider rate limits and outages?
questions.answer: Retry transient errors with exponential backoff and jitter, respect retry-after headers, queue non-urgent work, spread load across keys or regions where allowed, and fail over to a secondary model or provider with a tested prompt.

questions.question: How do you handle PII in AI systems?
questions.answer: Minimize what is sent, detect and redact or tokenize PII before prompts and logs, check provider data-retention and training terms, encrypt at rest and in transit, apply retention limits, and support deletion requests. Test redaction recall; missed PII in logs is a common leak.

questions.question: What is model or data drift, and how do you detect it?
questions.answer: The input distribution, user behavior or the provider model itself changes, and quality shifts. Detect it by monitoring input statistics and topics, eval scores on sampled traffic, user feedback and outcome metrics over time, and by pinning model versions so upgrades are deliberate.

questions.question: What does red-teaming an AI system involve?
questions.answer: Deliberately attacking the system before release: jailbreaks, prompt injection through every input channel, data exfiltration, harmful content, tool misuse and bias. Use a threat model, both automated attack generation and human testers, record findings with severity, fix, and turn findings into regression tests.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you can run red-teaming as a structured process tied to the actual product risks, not just a collection of jailbreak prompts.
framework: Scope: list the harms that matter for this product, such as data leaks, unsafe advice, unauthorized actions and policy violations.
Attack manually: jailbreaks, role-play, multi-turn escalation, and direct and indirect prompt injection through documents and tools.
Scale with automation: generate attack variations with models and fuzzing, and score results automatically.
Triage by severity and likelihood, fix with layered defenses, and re-test.
Keep successful attacks as regression tests and repeat before each major release.

follow_ups.q: Is red-teaming a one-time exercise?
follow_ups.a: No; models, prompts and tools change, so it is repeated before releases and the regression suite runs continuously.

common_mistakes: Testing only generic jailbreaks unrelated to the product's real risks.
Ignoring indirect injection through documents and tool outputs.
Fixing only by editing the system prompt.
Not turning findings into regression tests.

questions.question: What are guardrails, and where do they sit?
questions.answer: Checks around the model: input checks (policy, injection signals, PII), output checks (policy, schema, groundedness, sensitive data), and action checks (tool permissions, confirmations). Keep them independent of the main prompt so one failure does not disable all protection, and measure their false positive rate.

deep_dive.what_it_tests: Whether you see guardrails as layered controls around the model at specific points in the pipeline, and understand their trade-offs.
framework: Input layer: detect prompt injection, off-topic or abusive requests, and redact personal data where needed.
Retrieval and tools layer: permission filtering, least-privilege credentials and argument validation.
Output layer: schema validation, policy and safety classifiers, groundedness checks and PII leak detection.
Action layer: human approval for irreversible or high-value actions.
Operations: measure false positives and latency, log blocks, and tune thresholds.

follow_ups.q: Is a strong system prompt a guardrail?
follow_ups.a: It helps, but it can be overridden by injection, so real controls must live in code outside the model.

common_mistakes: Relying on the system prompt as the only guardrail.
Adding checks without measuring false positives and latency.
Forgetting tool permissions and action approval.
Using one layer and assuming it catches everything.

questions.question: How do you measure and reduce bias in an LLM feature?
questions.answer: Define the harms relevant to your use case, build test sets that vary protected attributes while holding the task constant, compare outcomes and error rates across groups, and review qualitatively. Reduce with better data, prompt and policy changes, and human review for high-stakes decisions.

questions.question: How do you deploy prompt or model changes safely?
questions.answer: Treat them like code: review, offline evals in CI, feature flags, canary or percentage rollout with automated rollback on metric drops, and versioned configs so any response can be traced to the exact prompt and model.

questions.question: Implement retry with exponential backoff for an LLM API call.
Write a structure-aware text chunker.
questions.answer:
Split on headings and blank lines first, then pack paragraphs into chunks up to a token budget, with a small overlap, and never split inside code blocks.

```python
def chunk(paragraphs, max_tokens=400, overlap=1, count=len):
    chunks, cur = [], []
    for p in paragraphs:
        if cur and sum(map(count, cur)) + count(p) > max_tokens:
            chunks.append('\n\n'.join(cur))
            cur = cur[-overlap:] if overlap else []
        cur.append(p)
    if cur:
        chunks.append('\n\n'.join(cur))
    return chunks
```

Pass a real tokenizer's length function as count; len counts characters.

questions.question: Implement hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion.
Parse and validate structured output from an LLM, with a repair retry.
Implement a token-bucket rate limiter for LLM calls.
questions.answer:
Limit both requests and tokens per minute, because providers enforce both.

```python
import time, threading
class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate_per_sec, capacity):
        self.rate, self.cap = rate_per_sec, capacity
        self.tokens, self.t = capacity, time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def acquire(self, n=1):
        while True:
            with self.lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self.tokens = min(self.cap, self.tokens + (now - self.t) * self.rate)
                self.t = now
                if self.tokens >= n:
                    self.tokens -= n
                    return
                wait = (n - self.tokens) / self.rate
            time.sleep(wait)
```

questions.question: Implement a minimal agent loop with tool calls and a step limit.
Implement a conversation-history manager that fits a token budget.
questions.answer:
Always keep the system prompt and the latest user turn; add earlier turns newest-first until the budget is reached; summarize what was dropped into one message.

```python
def fit_history(system, turns, budget, count, summarize):
    kept, used = [], count(system) + count(turns[-1])
    for t in reversed(turns[:-1]):
        if used + count(t) > budget * 0.8:
            break
        kept.insert(0, t); used += count(t)
    dropped = turns[:len(turns) - 1 - len(kept)]
    summary = [summarize(dropped)] if dropped else []
    return [system] + summary + kept + [turns[-1]]
```
